edges.effect_quant: The black cohosh literature is inconsistent. Some trials report improvement in hot flash number and severity, but larger placebo-controlled cancer-survivor and crossover trials found no significant advantage over placebo. In one recent 84-woman trial, symptom counts improved significantly versus placebo, while a 132-patient phase III crossover trial found a 17% reduction in frequency on black cohosh versus 26% on placebo.
edges.population: peri- or postmenopausal women using black cohosh to relieve vasomotor symptoms, including some women with a history of breast cancer
edges.mechanism: Black cohosh does not appear to act like a straightforward estrogen replacement. Proposed mechanisms include serotonergic or central thermoregulatory effects, which could plausibly influence vasomotor symptoms, but biologic uncertainty mirrors the uneven clinical results.
edges.summary: The most defensible interpretation is mixed. Smaller or selected trials sometimes suggest that black cohosh reduces hot flash frequency or severity, but better-controlled studies have repeatedly failed to show a clear benefit over placebo, leaving a possible small effect in some subgroups rather than a robust general solution.
edges.caveats: Formulations differ substantially across trials, and only some standardized extracts have been studied. Placebo responses in menopausal hot-flash trials are large, which makes modest benefits hard to distinguish from noise.

evidence.citation: Pockaj BA et al 2006 J Clin Oncol
evidence.notes: Phase III double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial of black cohosh in the management of hot flashes: NCCTG Trial N01CC1.

effect_quant.comparator: mean reduction in hot flash frequency on black cohosh over two 4-week treatment periods; placebo showed a 26% reduction over the same periods

evidence.citation: Shahnazi Mahnaz et al 2013 J Caring Sci
evidence.notes: Effect of black cohosh (cimicifuga racemosa) on vasomotor symptoms in postmenopausal women: a randomized clinical trial.
